segments.text: AI can sound incredibly patient, caring, and understanding.
We use it to answer questions,
bounce ideas around, and help organize our daily lives.
But we have to ask,
what happens when kind words simply aren't enough?
Let's say you're a student.
For the past two weeks,
you've been eating lunch completely alone at school.
You feel isolated and you're not sure what to do about it.
Present this scenario to two sources.
Your older sister says to sit with her.
The chatbot expresses sympathy and offers strategies.
But pan down to the truth underneath.
The chatbot offers comforting ideas,
but won't be in the cafeteria tomorrow.
Your sister is making physical room at her table.
This highlights a concept known as the support trap.
The support trap is mistaking an AI's supportive language
for actual, tangible support.
AI absolutely has a real use case in these situations.
It can help you understand your feelings,
organize your thoughts,
and practice what you want to say.
But it cannot take the place of a person
who genuinely cares about you.
If you only tell the chatbot about your lunch problem,
you might feel a little better that night.
But the next day, you'll still be sitting by yourself.
And the real people who could have actually helped you,
like your sister,
will never even know you wanted them there.
To use AI safely, we must understand its boundaries.
This guide categorizes AI into venting, preparation,
and danger.
Left is venting, a safe space to put frustration into words,
ending right inside the chat.
The middle is preparation.
Imagine dreading telling your mom about a bad grade.
AI helps you rehearse.
But there is a strict limitation to preparation.
The AI can definitely help you formulate
that difficult first sentence,
but the action must ultimately move outside the chat.
Your mom still needs to actually hear what you have to say from you.
The rule for these safe zones is straightforward.
Use AI to prepare for people rather than using it to replace them.
That leaves us with the final category, danger.
If someone is unsafe,
the absolute rule is that you must leave the chat immediately
and involve a real person.
To understand why this rule is so critical,
we have to look at a real world case.
Please note, the following story discusses suicide.
In 2025, a journalist named Laura Reevely
wrote about her 29-year-old daughter Sophie.
Sophie's family knew she was struggling with her mental health,
but they had no idea how deep her pain truly ran.
The hidden reality was that Sophie had been extensively documenting
her severe distress to chat GPT for months leading up to her death.
The AI responded exactly how it was programmed to.
It answered kindly and sometimes encouraged her to get help.
But it had a fatal flaw by design.
It was fundamentally incapable of picking up a phone to call her family,
and it could not alert her therapist to what she was sharing.
After Sophie died by suicide, her family discovered the chat logs.
Her mother described the AI interface as a black box.
The machine kept life-saving information completely hidden
from the actual human beings who could have intervened
and provided real help.
We can prevent this with three mandatory steps.
First, leave the chat.
Contact a trusted adult, 988 for crisis support,
or 911 for immediate danger.
Second, do it now.
Use this script.
I'm worried about my friend. Can you help?
Finally, tell anyway, even if sworn to secrecy.
In moments of crisis, there is one absolute moral rule you must follow.
Safety always outrank secrecy.
As this final banner states,
AI can help you get ready for people.
But in danger, leave the chat and bring in someone who can act.
